_comment: DRAFT - not wired into any loader. Successor to config/drafts/crops_earthlike_v1.json. Re-derived from config/drafts/ecocrop_source/cropbasics_scrape.csv.gz (2568 records x 63 cols, FAO datasheets scraped ~2023), NOT from the 2019 Recocrop table v1 used. Column mapping: Temp_Abs_Min/temp_opt_min/Temp_Opt_Max/Temp_Abs_Max -> temp_c; Rain_* -> precip_mm_yr; cycle_min/cycle_max -> cycle_days; pH_Abs_* -> soil_ph; Texture_Abs/drainage_abs/Fertility_Abs/Depth_Abs -> soil; Light_Abs_Max -> light_min; photoperiod -> photoperiod; Climate.Zone -> climate_zone (Koppen codes only). KILLING TEMPERATURE IS NOW SPLIT: Killing.temp..early.growth -> seasonality.frost_kills_at_c (actively growing tissue), Killing.temp..during.rest -> seasonality.winter_hardy_to_c (cold-hardened dormant plant), the latter nulled where the crop has no overwintering field phase. EcoCrop's not-assessed sentinel in these two columns is the literal string 'no input' (1410/2568 rows), NOT 0 - so a 0 here is a measurement and is preserved. notes_excerpt is a short quote from the joined crop_view_data.csv.gz Notes field. Yields, labor_days_ha, storage, products, processing_gate, package_tags, value_class, water{} and slot are AUTHORED, never EcoCrop. Attribution: FAO EcoCrop. See config/drafts/CROPS_V2_NOTES.md.

proposedGoods.rationale: Fermented grape must; the export half of Mediterranean polyculture. Carried from v1.
The other half of Mediterranean polyculture and the missing input to the existing 'soap' good. Carried from v1.
Generic pressed seed/fruit oil (linseed, sesame, rape, coconut, palm). Carried from v1.
Perishable orchard/vine output, deliberately near-untradeable. Carried from v1.
Raisins, figs, dates - the caravan-legal form of fruit. Carried from v1.
Northern-temperate analogue of wine (apple, pear). Carried from v1.
Non-cereal perishable staple (tubers, turnip). Carried from v1.
Straw, stover, haulm, hay, oilcake - the link between the crop and domesticate catalogues. Carried from v1.
Rope and rigging from hemp and coir; the agricultural input to the existing 'ships' good. Carried from v1.
Concentrated dye cake as distinct from raw 'dye_plants'. Carried from v1.

Dried legume seed. Storable protein with a completely different demand curve from grain, and the carrier of the nitrogen-fixation/rotation mechanic - nine catalogue crops currently have no good to sell.
Crystallised cane sugar. The archetypal gated plantation commodity: worthless as standing cane, imperially valuable after a mill. No existing good covers sweeteners at all.

Dried high-value-per-weight seasoning (pepper, cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, cardamom, ginger, turmeric, saffron, cumin, coriander). This is THE long-distance luxury trade good and the economy currently has only generic 'herbs'.
Reeled silk from mulberry leaf via sericulture. Highest value-to-bulk of any bulk-tradeable good; it is what makes an overland route across a continent pay for itself.
Cured leaf. Distinct from coffee in soil (obligate acid), climate (monsoon highland) and demand geography; currently collapsed into 'herbs', which erases both.
Fermented and dried cherry. Tropical-highland only, so it is an import for every temperate polity - a clean, geographically forced trade dependency.
Fermented cacao bean. Equatorial-lowland only and gated on controlled fermentation; also a fat source, which no other luxury is.
Cured leaf. Grows nearly anywhere warm but is worthless uncured, so its value lives entirely in a facility - the cleanest test case for the processing-gate mechanic on a luxury.
Shelled tree nuts. Dry, storable, high-fat, and unlike 'dried_fruit' they carry protein and oil - the orchard good that can actually provision a caravan or a siege.
Poppy latex. Extreme value-to-weight (0.02 t/ha) and doubles as the only analgesic input, so it has both a luxury and a medical demand channel.
Grain beer. v1 proposed wine and cider but left the barley/wheat belt with no fermented product; ale is also the historical form in which grain surplus becomes urban calories and tax.
Bagasse, stalk, husk and prunings. Named in the v1 schema example but never proposed as a good; it is what makes sugar milling and metalworking possible in a deforested tropical landscape.

crops.name: bread wheat
crops.notes_excerpt: Winter wheat may withstand -20 C in the early and dormant stages, later it is like spring wheat and is sensitive to frost.
crops.notes: ACOUP IVb: 14.25-19.5 labour-days/iugerum -> ~57-78 d/ha. The two-field split is visible here: winter_hardy -20 vs frost_kills 0.

crops.name: durum wheat
crops.notes: Driest-optimum wheat (ROPMX 700 vs bread wheat 900) and hottest (TOPMX 25). Semolina/pasta slot; killing temps not assessed by FAO.

crops.name: emmer
crops.notes: Hulled founder crop (SW Asian ubiquity 0.44). Needs dehusking labour a naked wheat does not; envelope is a shade cooler/drier than bread wheat.

crops.name: einkorn
crops.envelope_ref: estimated - no Triticum monococcum record in the 2023 EcoCrop scrape; envelope shifted from Triticum dicoccon (emmer) toward poorer/colder ground per the founder-crop literature
crops.notes: ESTIMATED. The poorest-soil founder cereal (ubiquity 0.34); its slot is marginal upland ground where emmer fails, not a yield advantage.

crops.name: barley
crops.notes_excerpt: The main climatic mishap is frost damage to the seedlings, when the death of many plants can drastically thin out the crop.
crops.notes: Garnsey ordering confirmed: RMIN 200 vs bread wheat 300. ACOUP: ~2/3 the labour, ~35% fewer calories than wheat.

crops.name: rye
crops.notes_excerpt: Autumn sown cultivars require exposure to low temperatures as a prerequisite to flowering; seedlings of winter rye may tolerate -18 C.
crops.notes: EcoCrop lists PP short-day; rye is a long-day cereal. The crop the KTMP bug hid: winter_hardy -18 vs frost_kills -1. Widest drainage tolerance of the cereals. Vernalization-obligate when autumn sown.

crops.name: oats
crops.notes_excerpt: Winter varieties are sown in areas with relatively mild winters while spring varieties are used where winters are more severe.
crops.notes: The horse-fodder cereal; its slot is cool wet oceanic ground plus the draught-animal feed chain.

crops.name: rice
crops.notes: EcoCrop indica. DRAR poorly-drained-only is the paddy signature and the only obligate-impeded-drainage crop in the catalogue.

crops.name: maize
crops.notes_excerpt: It is easily killed by frost.
crops.notes: GMIN 65 / GMAX 365 is EcoCrop's known-absurd duration range (flagged in G1a); treat cycle_days as advisory for maize only. Nixtamalization gate per G1a.

crops.name: sorghum
crops.notes: Grain-sorghum record (ROPMX 600) rather than the sweet-sorghum record (ROPMX 1000): the dryland staple, not the syrup crop.

crops.name: pearl millet
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = 2 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes: RMIN 200 and a 60-day floor: the shortest-season drought escape in the catalogue. Seed-retention penalty per G1a (African millets keep 1-3% of harvest, not 20-30%).

crops.name: foxtail millet
crops.notes: The East Asian loess-belt millet: cooler than pearl millet (TOPMN 16 vs 25) and the only cereal that will start in a cold continental spring on 300 mm. Proso millet (Panicum miliaceum) occupies the same slot with a shorter cycle if a steppe variant is wanted.

crops.name: buckwheat
crops.notes: Not a grass. GMAX 85 days makes it the emergency catch crop: sown after a failed cereal, harvested before frost. Also the only pseudocereal that tolerates acid podzol.

crops.name: teff
crops.notes: Ethiopian highland cereal; TMIN 2 with TOPMN 22 is an unusual combination that maps onto tropical highlands specifically. Seed retention ~1% (G1a) - the most extreme in the catalogue.

crops.name: lentil
crops.notes_excerpt: Early cultivars growing 70-120 days, late cultivars 120-130 days, or sown in the autumn 180-240 days.
crops.notes: SW Asian founder crop, ubiquity 0.68 - tied with barley as the most reliably present. Nitrogen fixation: the rotation partner for autumn-sown wheat.

crops.name: chickpea
crops.notes: winter_hardy -9 with frost_kills 0: the Mediterranean autumn-sown pulse that survives the winter but not a spring frost. Ubiquity ~0.15 (G1a) - a late, patchy founder-crop arrival.

crops.name: pea
crops.notes: TOPMN 10 is the coldest pulse optimum here: the northern-European rotation legume where chickpea and lentil both fail.

crops.name: faba bean
crops.notes_excerpt: Spring cultivars may survive -10 C but are damaged by late frost.
crops.notes: Highest-yielding and most nitrogen-productive of the temperate pulses; the heavy-clay pulse (Texture heavy,medium). Killing temps not assessed by FAO despite the Notes quoting -10.

crops.name: common bean
crops.notes: New World pulse, the third of the three sisters (only ~2,500 BP per G1a - do not emit it with maize and squash at t=0).

crops.name: cowpea
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = -1 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes: GMIN 30 days and RMIN 300: the hot-dry pulse that intercrops with pearl millet and sorghum. No temperate analogue.

crops.name: soybean
crops.notes: The only pulse in the catalogue that is simultaneously an oilseed and a fermentation substrate (shoyu/miso/tofu); that triple product is its non-substitutable slot.

crops.name: bitter vetch
crops.notes: Founder crop (ubiquity 0.22) that is famine food and fodder rather than a table pulse - the seed must be soaked to remove the toxic amino acids. Envelope is the driest/poorest of the pulses.

crops.name: white lupin
crops.notes: The acid-sand pulse: fixes nitrogen where nothing else will and is the classic green-manure legume. Alkaloid bitterness makes the leaching gate absolute, not merely economic.

crops.name: alfalfa
crops.notes_excerpt: Winter-hardy types suited to cold regions have a longer dormancy period and shorter growing season than the less winter-hardy types.
crops.notes: winter_hardy -25 is the second-coldest in the catalogue and is what makes it a true multi-year ley. Deep taproot + irrigation_response 0.75: the crop that turns an irrigated oasis into a cavalry base.

crops.name: red clover
crops.notes: The nitrogen course of the Norfolk four-course rotation. Shorter-lived and wetter-tolerant than alfalfa (RMIN 300, TOPMX 25) - it works in oceanic temperate where lucerne rots.

crops.name: common vetch
crops.notes: The over-winter green-manure course: sown into stubble, ploughed under or cut before the spring cereal. Distinct from bitter vetch (a seed crop) and clover (a multi-year ley).

crops.name: turnip
crops.notes_excerpt: Roots also grown for feeding to livestock during fall and winter; hardened winter turnip can survive short periods of exposure to -15 to -20 C.
crops.notes: The root course of the Norfolk rotation and the reason winter stall-feeding is possible: it is the only crop here that stores standing in the field through frost.

crops.name: potato
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = -1 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes: Lowland/temperate potato. Calories per hectare beat any cereal here, but shelf_life 150 d and form 'cellared' keep it out of the long-haul trade network - that asymmetry is the point.

crops.name: bitter potato
crops.notes: Solanum x juzepczukii, the actual chuno cultivar - TOPMN 6 / TOPMX 14 is the coldest optimum of any crop in the catalogue and it is glycoalkaloid-bitter raw. Unlike S. tuberosum the gate is 'any', not 'staple': without freeze-drying this crop is simply not food. This replaces v1's mislabelled 'highland_tuber'.

crops.name: sweet potato
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = 1 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes: No processing gate and an 80-day floor: the crop that gets planted after a typhoon or a war. Its historical role is famine insurance, and per G1a an incumbent yam blocks its adoption.

crops.name: cassava
crops.notes_excerpt: May not tolerate 7 C for prolonged periods and it is easily killed by frost.
crops.notes: Shelf life of days in the ground-to-mouth state; the processed form is the only tradeable one. Tolerates the poorest acid soils of any staple here (Fertility_Abs low, pH from 4.5).

crops.name: white yam
crops.notes: The West African forest-margin staple and the highest-labour root here (mound-building and staking). Unlike cassava it stores for months without processing, which is why it holds the niche against sweet potato (G1a incumbency).

crops.name: taro
crops.notes_excerpt: Require at least 180-210 frost-free days a year; the tubers are grated and fermented to make poi.
crops.notes: The only tuber that shares rice's waterlogging tolerance - it is the wet-terrace staple of the Pacific and the pondfield analogue of paddy. Calcium-oxalate acridity is handled by cooking, not a tech gate.

crops.name: banana
crops.notes: Musa acuminata x balbisiana - the AAB/ABB cooking-banana hybrid, i.e. plantain, not the dessert clone. Vegetatively propagated: it moves as living suckers, so its diffusion follows people, not seed-grain trade.

crops.name: coconut
crops.notes: Salt-tolerant coastal palm: the only crop in the catalogue that prefers a beach. Its four-product fan-out (food, oil, coir rigging, thatch) makes it the tropical equivalent of the olive.

crops.name: oil palm
crops.notes: Highest oil yield per hectare of any crop here by roughly 5x. RMIN 1000 with RMAX 8000 makes it an equatorial-rainforest-only good, so it is a pure export commodity for anyone outside that band.

crops.name: sugarcane
crops.notes_excerpt: There are large varietal differences in cold tolerance and susceptibility to frost.
crops.notes: The archetypal gated crop: chewable cane is a snack, crystallised sugar is an empire. labor_days_ha 200 plus the mill is why this crop historically implies coerced labour.

crops.name: olive
crops.notes_excerpt: It requires a long, hot growing season, no late spring frosts to kill the blossoms and sufficient winter chill to insure fruit set.
crops.notes: Now shows winter_hardy -10 / frost_kills 0 - the split finally expresses what v1 could not. Real limiter per G1a is still catastrophic-frost RETURN PERIOD (>10 yr), a call-site check.

crops.name: sesame
crops.notes: The hot-dry oilseed: GMIN 40 days on 300 mm. The oldest oil crop in the Old World and the only edible oil available to an arid lowland with no olive.

crops.name: rapeseed
crops.notes_excerpt: Unhardened plants can survive -4 C, fully-hardened spring type -10 to -12 C, and hardened winter rapeseed short periods of -15 to -20 C.
crops.notes: winter_hardy -15 / frost_kills -6: the only oilseed that overwinters in a boreal climate, and therefore the northern lamp-oil crop where olive is impossible.

crops.name: sunflower
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = -10 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes: TMAX 45 with RMIN 300: the continental-steppe oilseed. During-rest -10 is EcoCrop's seed figure, not a field hardiness, so winter_hardy_to_c is null (spring-sown annual).

crops.name: safflower
crops.notes_excerpt: Seedling in the rosette leafy state is frost-resistant to -7 to -14 C depending on the varieties, after this stage frost below -2 C may destroy the plant.
crops.notes: Dual-slot: deep-rooted dryland oilseed AND the only red/yellow dye that is also a food crop. The rosette-vs-bolted hardiness gap (-14 vs -2) is the clearest case in the catalogue of why the two-field split matters.

crops.name: castor
crops.notes: Non-food oil: lamp fuel, lubricant, leather dressing, purgative. edible 'none' on every product is deliberate - ricin. Its slot is industrial oil in a hot climate with no whales.

crops.name: flax
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = -6 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes_excerpt: Seedlings may survive -6 to -11 C, but mature plants may not tolerate frost.
crops.notes: Fertility_Abs 'high' is the only such rating among the field crops - it earns its reputation for exhausting soil. Retting requires standing water, which couples linen production to river/pond access.

crops.name: cotton
crops.notes: Old World Gossypium herbaceum, not American upland. TMIN 18 is the highest cold floor of any field crop here: cotton cannot start in a temperate spring at all.

crops.name: hemp
crops.notes: cordage is the non-substitutable slot: rigging is what couples this crop to the existing 'ships' strategic good. Tolerates poor drainage, unlike flax.

crops.name: jute
crops.notes_excerpt: Yields may be about 34 t/ha of green plants giving 2 t/ha of dry retted fiber.
crops.notes: Highest fibre tonnage per hectare in the catalogue and the cheapest. Its slot is sacking and bulk packaging - it is the good that makes long-distance grain and sugar shipment physically possible.

crops.name: ramie
crops.notes: Perennial, 4-6 cuts a year (GMIN 45 with GMAX 365). Strongest and whitest plant fibre known but the gum makes degumming labour brutal - which is exactly why it stayed a Chinese speciality good rather than a commodity.

crops.name: grape
crops.notes: EcoCrop lists PP short-day; Vitis vinifera fruits reliably to ~51N (Mosel). winter_hardy -20 / frost_kills -3 is the split that lets a vine survive a continental winter but lose a crop to a May frost - the single most important fact about viticulture's northern limit.

crops.name: fig
crops.notes: light_min 0.35 - the most shade-tolerant Mediterranean tree here, so it works as an interplant in an olive grove rather than competing for the same ground.

crops.name: date palm
crops.notes: EcoCrop lists PP short-day; the date palm fruits fine at 25-35N. TMAX 52 C, the highest heat ceiling in the catalogue, on RMAX 400 mm with irrigation_response 0.95: it wants heat and a water table, not rain. That is the oasis in two numbers.

crops.name: apple
crops.notes: winter_hardy -30 is the coldest tree here; it is the fruit slot for climates where the vine cannot ripen. Chilling requirement is real but unquantified by EcoCrop - a call-site check.

crops.name: pear
crops.notes: winter_hardy -34, the coldest value in the whole catalogue, with TOPMX 35 - a wider tolerance than apple at both ends but drier (RMAX 2100 vs 3200), so it takes the continental slot apple does not.

crops.name: pomegranate
crops.notes: Salt- and drought-tolerant with a 120-day shelf life on the whole fruit - the only fresh fruit here that can actually be carried by caravan. Rind is a tannin/dye source, which is why it turns up in leatherworking regions.

crops.name: citrus
crops.notes: winter_hardy -10 / frost_kills 0 defines the citrus belt exactly: it survives a cold night in dormancy and dies to a frost in flower. Peel oil is the crop's link to the existing 'perfumes' luxury good.

crops.name: almond
crops.notes: Earliest-flowering tree in the catalogue (TOPMN 12), which is precisely its weakness: winter_hardy -5 but frost_kills -1, so a late frost takes the whole crop. Highest-value dryland tree nut.

crops.name: walnut
crops.notes: Four-product tree: nut, oil, brown dye, and the highest-value cabinet timber in the catalogue. winter_hardy -24 puts it well north of the almond.

crops.name: chestnut
crops.notes: The 'bread tree': ground chestnut flour is a genuine cereal substitute, which is why it maps to 'grain' and carries value_class staple. Acid-soil mountain slot where no cereal is worth sowing; labour is low because there is no annual tillage.

crops.name: hazelnut
crops.notes: TOPMN 10 and RMIN 600: the oceanic-temperate nut, and the only one whose byproduct is coppice rod (hurdles, wattle) rather than sawn timber.

crops.name: pistachio
crops.notes: RMIN 250 with winter_hardy -18: needs a cold winter AND a hot dry summer, a combination only continental steppe margins offer. The highest value-per-tonne food crop in the catalogue after the spices.

crops.name: melon
crops.notes: An irrigated garden crop, not a field crop: 50-120 day cycle, irrigation_response 0.8. Its slot is peri-urban market gardening - the thing grown on the good watered land next to a city.

crops.name: tea
crops.notes: PHMAX 6.0 - the only obligate-acid-soil crop in the catalogue, which is a real placement constraint given we model soil pH. Perennial with a 40-year stand: planting tea is a multi-generation land commitment.

crops.name: coffee
crops.notes: TOPMN 14 / TOPMX 28 with TMAX 34 is a narrow band, and combined with the altitude envelope it only lands on tropical highlands - the classic coffee-belt geometry. Never lowland-tropical.

crops.name: cacao
crops.notes_excerpt: Temperatures of about 5 C, even for a short period, may damage cacao; the tree is damaged by frost.
crops.notes: frost_kills 0 but winter_hardy +5: it dies well above freezing. Narrowest usable band in the catalogue and shade-demanding (light_min 0.35), so it is an understorey crop of the equatorial lowland only.

crops.name: tobacco
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = -3 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes_excerpt: The leaves are cured and dried; very sensitive to frost and the duration of the frost-free period is an important production factor.
crops.notes: Widest package_tags of any luxury here (70-150 day cycle, RMIN 350) - it will grow almost anywhere warm, which is exactly why it became a mass colonial cash crop rather than a rarity. Value is entirely in the curing barn.

crops.name: opium poppy
crops.notes_excerpt: Annual, grown as a winter crop in the subtropics it require 135-170 days to mature and as a summer crop in temperate areas it require 150-210 days.
crops.notes: Highest value-to-weight ratio in the catalogue (0.02 t/ha at value_mult 60) and the highest labour, because lancing capsules is entirely hand work. Also the only medicinal analgesic source - it has a non-luxury demand too.

crops.name: black pepper
crops.notes: RMIN 2000 mm/yr is the wettest requirement in the catalogue and light_min 0.35 makes it an understorey vine on living supports. Together those two facts confine it to a handful of wet tropical coasts - which is the entire economic history of the spice trade in one envelope.

crops.name: cinnamon
crops.notes: TMIN 18 with RMIN 1200: true cinnamon is a wet equatorial island crop (Ceylon), which is why cassia (Cinnamomum cassia, TMIN 10, RMIN 900) was the mainland substitute. Harvest destroys the coppice shoot, so yield is bound to a 2-year cutting cycle.

crops.name: clove
crops.notes: TMIN 20 is the highest cold floor of any crop in the catalogue - it will not grow outside a genuinely equatorial maritime climate. This is the crop that justifies monopoly geography (the Moluccas problem).

crops.name: nutmeg
crops.notes: The one crop that yields two separately-priced spices from one fruit (nutmeg kernel and mace aril) - the clearest product fan-out in the catalogue. Same equatorial-island confinement as clove.

crops.name: ginger
crops.notes: The tradeable rhizome: unlike a leaf or a berry it ships as a living propagule, which is why ginger diffused out of Asia centuries before pepper cultivation did. Shade-tolerant, so it interplants under tree crops.

crops.name: turmeric
crops.notes: Dual spice/dye slot, and the only yellow dye in the catalogue that is also a foodstuff and a preservative. TMIN 18 keeps it strictly tropical, so temperate regions must import it or use safflower.

crops.name: cardamom
crops.notes: ROPMX 6000 mm/yr is the highest optimum rainfall of any crop here, and it wants shade at altitude - a wet tropical montane forest understorey and nothing else. Second only to saffron in value per tonne.

crops.name: saffron
crops.notes_excerpt: Frosts and rains during the flowering are harmful and can damage the crop.
crops.notes: TOPMN 7 / TOPMX 19 makes saffron the ONE temperate-dryland luxury spice - every other spice here is tropical, so this is the slot a Mediterranean or steppe polity can actually occupy in the luxury trade. 12 kg/ha at 380 labour-days is by far the worst labour-to-mass ratio in the catalogue, and correct.

crops.name: cumin
crops.notes: GMIN 60 days: a short-season irrigated dryland seed spice. Together with coriander it gives arid regions a domestic spice trade that does not depend on tropical imports.

crops.name: coriander
crops.notes: GMIN 35 days, the shortest cycle in the catalogue, and winter_hardy -10: it fits into gaps in a rotation that nothing else will. Dual leaf/seed product with completely different shelf lives.

crops.name: madder
crops.envelope_ref: estimated - Rubia tinctorum is present in EcoCrop (code 9344) but carries NO envelope values at all; numbers from standard dye-plant horticultural practice (deep friable calcareous loam, 2-3 year root crop, frost-hardy perennial rootstock)
crops.notes: ESTIMATED envelope - EcoCrop has the species but no numbers. The red half of the dye triad; deep-dug root lifted in year 2-3, which is what ratoon_cycles 2 encodes.

crops.name: indigo
crops.notes_excerpt: North of Equator seed are sown in October or April, and the crop ripen in June-July.
crops.notes: 50:1 mass reduction from leaf to cake - the clearest case in the catalogue of value living in processing, not the plant. Also a nitrogen-fixing legume, so it belongs in a rotation as well as a vat.

crops.name: woad
crops.envelope_ref: estimated - Isatis tinctoria is entirely absent from the 2023 EcoCrop scrape; envelope from standard European dye-plant practice (biennial, calcareous loam, cool-summer temperate, 2-3 cuts per season)
crops.notes: ESTIMATED envelope - not in EcoCrop at all. Kept because it is the ONLY blue dye available to a temperate region: without it, blue cloth must be imported from the indigo tropics, which is a real and legible trade dependency. Notoriously soil-exhausting, hence fertility_min 0.55.

crops.name: mulberry
crops.notes_excerpt: Killed below -5 C and damaged by frost; the tree is dormant below 13 C.
crops.notes: The catalogue's one crop whose principal product is not made of the plant: leaves feed Bombyx mori and the good is silk. The gate is therefore a whole domesticate-plus-facility chain, and it is the single strongest justification for a long-distance luxury trade route.

crops.name: quinoa
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = -8 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes: KTMP -8 on BOTH columns (a rare case where FAO assessed them equal) with TOPMX 18: the cold-hardiest and most salt-tolerant seed crop here. Saponin washing is a product process, not a gate - it costs water and labour but no tech.

crops.name: amaranth
crops.killing_temp_note: EcoCrop 'Killing temp. during rest' = 4 C is recorded but this crop has no overwintering field phase, so winter_hardy_to_c is null per the v2 rule.
crops.notes: Amaranthus caudatus (kiwicha). Dual grain/leaf-vegetable product and a C4 pathway, so unlike quinoa it keeps yielding at TOPMX 28 - the two Andean pseudocereals cover different altitude bands rather than duplicating.
